lesson_title: How a Footpath Becomes a Canyon
hook_text: Some Eastern Cape canyons are deep enough to hide a truck. Almost every one of them began as a footpath.
clip_script: Erosion follows a script, and any overstocked camp will perform it for you. Act one: too many cattle, too little grass — overgrazing — and a bare patch appears. Act two: rain arrives on the naked ground like a hail of tiny hammers, each drop splashing particles loose. Act three: the trampled, compacted surface refuses to drink, so the water travels — first as a thin silent sheet that shaves the whole surface a millimetre at a time. Act four: the sheet organises itself into finger-width channels — rills — shallow enough to step over and easy to ignore. Act five: the rills merge and bite deeper with every storm, until one season the farmer finds a donga across the camp — a raw canyon with vertical walls, eating the field that fed a household. And the path the herd walked to water every day, packed hard as a stoep floor? It was the original drain. A great many dongas were born as footpaths. One further act, because history acts in South Africa's version: the apartheid homeland map squeezed people and cattle onto the smallest, weakest land — which is why the deepest dongas today run through those former districts. A past cause wearing a present scar. And remember the exchange rate underneath it all: soil builds at a teaspoon a year and washes away by the bucket.
visual_style: Time-lapse sketch of a green camp: a bare patch spreading, animated raindrops hammering, a silver sheet of water creeping, finger rills branching, then the ground tearing open into a cliff-walled donga beside a hardened cattle path; a final overlay of a teaspoon against a tipping bucket.
mood: Quiet menace building act by act, ending on sober awe.
pacing: Slow ominous open, accelerating beats through the five acts, a hard stop at the opened donga.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn the stitches that close the canyon.
